passage: At the village anganwadi, three toddlers sat in a row on the mat with their steel plates. Urmila, the oldest, banged her spoon on her plate. Clang! Little Sabina watched, then banged hers too, grinning. Soon the boy beside her was banging as well. When Urmila pushed away her bitter gourd, Sabina pushed hers away too, though she had eaten it happily the day before. The anganwadi didi laughed and gave each of them a piece of banana.

qa.q: What did Urmila bang on her plate?
qa.a: Her spoon.

qa.q: Why did Sabina push away her bitter gourd?
qa.a: Sabina was simply copying Urmila, feeling playful and delighted by the game, not disliking the food, since she had eaten it happily the day before.

qa.q: What could the anganwadi didi try next time with the bitter gourd?
qa.a: Eat a piece cheerfully herself, or seat Sabina beside a child who is eating it, since the toddlers copy what they see.

qa.q: How might the anganwadi didi see the banging?
qa.a: Probably amused, seeing it as a playful copying game spreading down the row.

grounding: Toddlers copy each other's spoon-banging and food refusal as pure imitation, without any sense of rules.

passage: On the first day after the holidays at the village school, Charu, Deepu and Munni all had green water bottles from the Tuesday market. Kishore's was red. He hid it behind his back. At break, the three friends played 'tractor' with their green bottles as wheels, and Kishore stood and watched. That evening he cried until his mother promised to go to the market. 'Red is nice too,' she said. 'No! Everyone has green!' On Tuesday, holding his new green bottle, Kishore ran straight to join the tractor game.

qa.q: Where did the green water bottles come from?
qa.a: The Tuesday market.

qa.q: Why did Kishore hide his red bottle?
qa.a: He felt left out and embarrassed because his bottle was different from everyone else's.

qa.q: How could Kishore's mother or teacher help him feel included without buying the same things?
qa.a: Help him join the tractor game with his red bottle, showing that different colours can still play together.

qa.q: How might Charu see Kishore's new green bottle?
qa.a: Charu may simply be happy to have him join the game, perhaps without noticing how much the colour mattered to him.

grounding: A young child insists on the same bottle colour as his friends, because being different feels like being left out.

passage: Monday: Harish came to school humming the song from Chotu the Elephant, his favourite cartoon. Sonali laughed. 'That's for babies!' The boys around her laughed too. Harish went red and stopped humming. Wednesday: when Mohan asked what everyone watched after school, Harish said, 'Cricket highlights,' and the others nodded. It felt good not to be laughed at, and also a bit like lying to himself. Saturday: at home, Harish watched Chotu the Elephant with the sound low, so nobody passing the window would hear. His little sister sang along loudly. He almost told her to stop, then quietly hummed with her.

qa.q: What did Harish say he watched after school?
qa.a: Cricket highlights.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after giving the cricket answer?
qa.a: Relieved not to be laughed at, but also a little guilty, as if lying to himself.

qa.q: What small step could help Harish keep his own taste?
qa.a: Share it with one friend who might like it too, and remember that liking a cartoon isn't babyish.

qa.q: How might Sonali see her 'That's for babies!' comment?
qa.a: She may think it was a harmless joke, not realising it made Harish hide something he loved.

grounding: Over a week a child stops admitting he likes a cartoon after classmates mock it, feeling relief and a small self-betrayal.

subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]
passage: In Class 5, our teacher asked, 'Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?' I knew the answer: they weigh the same. Both are a kilo. But Abhinav shouted, 'Iron!' and then almost everyone said iron. Ma'am asked for hands. I looked around. Thirty hands up for iron. Mine stayed down for a second, and then I put it up too. Ma'am smiled and said, 'Both weigh the same.' My stomach dropped. I had known! I'm Pranav, and after that day I wrote my answer down before looking at anyone else's hand.

qa.q: What was the right answer?
qa.a: Both weigh the same; both are a kilo.

qa.q: Why did Pranav put a hand up for iron?
qa.a: Pranav felt unsure and nervous about being the only one, so doubting felt easier than standing alone.

qa.q: What did Pranav decide to do after that day?
qa.a: Write the answer down before looking at anyone else's hand.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel after Ma'am gave the answer?
qa.a: Probably a little embarrassed, since Abhinav's loud answer had led the class the wrong way.

grounding: A child who knew the right answer changes it when most of the class says otherwise.

passage: In his first week at the Mumbai school, Jeevan opened his steel tiffin at lunch: puttu and kadala curry, packed by his grandmother. Sachin wrinkled his nose. 'What's that, sawdust?' The whole table laughed. When Jeevan answered a question in class, a few boys copied his accent. By Friday, Jeevan was eating lunch in the corridor. On Monday he asked his mother to pack bread and jam, 'like everyone else'. She looked at him for a long moment. Jeevan didn't say why. He just stared at the puttu mould on the kitchen shelf, feeling angry and small at the same time.

qa.q: What was in Jeevan's tiffin?
qa.a: Puttu and kadala curry, packed by his grandmother.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he stared at the puttu mould?
qa.a: Angry and small at the same time, hurt by the teasing and resentful of having to change.

qa.q: What could Jeevan's mother do after his request?
qa.a: Gently ask what happened at school, and let his teacher know about the teasing so it can be stopped.

qa.q: How might Sachin see his 'sawdust' joke?
qa.a: As just a funny line that made the table laugh, not noticing it pushed Jeevan into the corridor.

grounding: A child laughed at for his homemade tiffin and accent shrinks and tries to copy the group, quietly resentful.

passage: Samir, you asked why I changed so much in Class 10. Honestly? Aditi was trying to be someone else. The new group said 'bro' about everything, so I said 'bro'. They all wore the same oversized hoodies, so I begged Mummy for one. Then one of the older boys started daring us to ride pillion on his bike without a helmet, fast, down the flyover. Everyone did it. I did it too, once, holding on so tight my fingers hurt, pretending to scream with joy. That night I realised none of them knew I love chemistry, or that I'm scared of speed. They knew my hoodie. I told Mummy about the bike rides that night, and she phoned the class teacher before we slept; the rides stopped that week. I still wear the hoodie sometimes. I don't ride that bike.

qa.q: What did the older boy dare them to do?
qa.a: Ride pillion on his bike without a helmet, fast, down the flyover.

qa.q: What did Aditi realise that night?
qa.a: Aditi felt uneasy and lonely, realising the group knew the hoodie but not the real Aditi, who loves chemistry and fears speed.

qa.q: What protective step followed Aditi telling Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy phoned the class teacher that same night, and the rides stopped that week.

qa.q: How might the others in the group have felt riding the bike?
qa.a: Some may have been as scared as Aditi but hid it too, all pretending to enjoy it in order to belong.

grounding: A teenager takes up a group's slang, clothes and risky dares to belong, while privately doubting it and feeling unknown.

passage: It was the last period before the exam holidays, the fans in Class 10C had stopped working, and the room was an oven. Vaibhav leaned over. 'Everyone's bunking maths and going to the chaat corner. Coming?' Urmila looked around. Half the back row was packing up. 'Everyone?' 'Everyone who matters,' Vaibhav said, grinning. 'Unless you want to sit here with the nerds.' Her face went hot. Missing one class didn't seem like much. Being left out of the group photo later felt enormous. She thought of the revision the teacher had promised to go through today. Her hand hovered over her bag. Then Nisha, from the front row, turned round. 'I'm staying. Sit with me?' Urmila let out a breath and stayed. Vaibhav rolled his eyes.

qa.q: Where were the students going if they bunked maths?
qa.a: To the chaat corner.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's face go hot?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious at the hint that staying would leave her out with 'the nerds'.

qa.q: What helped Urmila resist the pressure?
qa.a: Nisha's invitation to sit together, one ally, and remembering the revision promised for that day.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel when Urmila stays?
qa.a: Irritated or let down, rolling his eyes because his 'everyone' claim didn't work.

grounding: A teenager on a hot, restless day is told everyone is bunking class, with a hint of exclusion, and the social threat feels bigger than the act.

subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]
passage: In the school hall at the parent-teacher meeting, Hansa waited with her daughter Jahnavi on the plastic chairs, and noticed how much had changed in three months. Jahnavi's old friend Pinky was sitting across the hall with her mother, but Jahnavi didn't look at her. Instead she kept waving at three girls near the door, all with the same short haircut she'd had done last month. She said 'no cap' and 'lowkey' in every sentence, and one earbud played music Hansa had never heard. Hansa's first thought was to joke about her daughter's 'new language'. She didn't. She asked, 'Who are they? Tell me about them.' Jahnavi hesitated, then talked about them all the way to the class teacher's table, and even let Hansa hear the song.

qa.q: How many girls near the door did Jahnavi wave at?
qa.a: Three girls.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling as she noticed the changes?
qa.a: Curious and a little unsettled, and tempted to joke about Jahnavi's 'new language'.

qa.q: Why was asking 'Tell me about them' wiser than joking?
qa.a: Curiosity kept Jahnavi talking and even sharing the song, while ridicule could have pushed her further into the group and away from Hansa.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when Hansa asked about the new friends?
qa.a: Surprised and then pleased, since she hesitated but chose to talk and share her music.

grounding: A mother notices her teenager's new slang, music and friends, and chooses curiosity over ridicule.

passage: On the society terrace after the Class 11 farewell, someone produced a cigarette and passed it round the circle of eight. When it reached Pankaj, he just smiled and said, 'Nah, I'm good,' and passed it on. No speech. A couple of boys said, 'Ooh, good boy,' and laughed. Pankaj shrugged and went back to his cold drink. Ujjwal, next in line, looked at the cigarette, then at Pankaj. 'Same. I'm good too.' The teasing lasted maybe ten seconds before the talk moved on to cricket. Later, walking home, Ujjwal said, 'I've been wanting to say no for months. Didn't want to be the only one.' Pankaj grinned. 'Now there's two of us.'

qa.q: What did Pankaj say when the cigarette reached him?
qa.a: 'Nah, I'm good.'

qa.q: What had Ujjwal been feeling before that night?
qa.a: Ujjwal had wanted to refuse for months but felt afraid of being the only one.

qa.q: What made Pankaj's refusal work?
qa.a: It was relaxed and short, with no lecture, so the teasing faded fast and Ujjwal felt able to join in.

qa.q: How might the boys who teased Pankaj see the moment later?
qa.a: They may have forgotten it quickly, since there was no lecture to react to and the talk moved on to cricket.

grounding: A teenager refuses lightly, without a lecture, and one friend joins him, making it far easier to hold out.

passage: Baljeet arrived at the Pune hostel in the middle of the monsoon, knowing nobody, with a phone that barely held a charge and his family three states away. By the second week he was up till three every night, because that's when Wing C came alive: card games, loud debates, instant noodles on a smuggled heater. The seniors drank on Saturdays, and Baljeet, who had never touched alcohol, held a glass he didn't drink so he'd fit in. He began repeating their opinions on everything from cricket to politics. Mid-term exams were ten days away. One night his roommate Omkar, who went to bed at eleven, said, 'You don't even like cards.' Baljeet laughed it off, but lying awake later, he couldn't remember the last opinion he'd had that was really his.

qa.q: Until what time was Baljeet up every night?
qa.a: Till three.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel lying awake at the end?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit lost, unable to remember the last opinion that was truly his.

qa.q: What could Baljeet try to find himself again?
qa.a: Set a bedtime before the exams, keep one or two of his own habits, and spend time with people like Omkar who notice who he really is.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Baljeet's first weeks?
qa.a: Omkar seems to notice Baljeet changing to fit Wing C and is quietly concerned, pointing out he doesn't even like cards.

grounding: Away from family, a new hostel student drifts into the group's late nights, drinking habits and opinions, and loses track of himself.
